titleStmt.title: A Lightweight Approach to Network Intrusion Detection Using Machine Learning

analytic.title: A Lightweight Approach to Network Intrusion Detection Using Machine Learning

p.s: Network intrusion detection systems (IDS) play an important role in protecting modern computer networks from malicious activities.
However, machine-learning-based IDS solutions can require significant computational resources and large training datasets.
This paper presents a lightweight intrusion detection approach based on a Random Forest classifier and a small set of network traffic features.
The proposed approach extracts five features from network flows, including packet count, byte count, flow duration, source port, and destination port.
Experiments on a small benchmark dataset show that the proposed model can achieve competitive classification performance while maintaining a relatively low computational cost.
The results indicate that lightweight machine learning can be useful for intrusion detection in resource-constrained environments.
The rapid growth of computer networks and Internet-connected devices has increased the number and complexity of cybersecurity threats.
Attackers may exploit vulnerable services, steal sensitive information, or disrupt network operations.
Therefore, organizations require effective mechanisms for detecting suspicious network activities.
An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) monitors network or system activities and attempts to identify malicious behavior.
Traditional IDS solutions commonly rely on predefined signatures.
Although signature-based detection is effective for known attacks, it may have limited ability to identify previously unseen attack patterns [1].
Machine learning provides an alternative approach by learning patterns from historical network traffic.
Several studies have demonstrated that supervised learning algorithms can be applied to classify network connections as normal or malicious [2], [3].
However, many machine-learning solutions use a large number of features, which can increase computational cost.
This paper investigates a lightweight machine-learning approach for network intrusion detection.
The main objective is to determine whether a small number of easily extracted network features can provide useful classification performance.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 discusses related work.
Section 3 presents the proposed methodology.
Section 4 describes the experimental results.
Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper.
Machine learning has been widely investigated for intrusion detection.
According to Buczak and Guven [2], supervised learning algorithms such as decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks can be applied to detect abnormal network behavior.
Random Forest is particularly suitable for classification tasks because it combines multiple decision trees and can reduce the risk of overfitting.
Zhang et al. [3] showed that ensemble-based methods can achieve strong performance on network intrusion datasets.
Deep learning has also been applied to intrusion detection.
For example, Yin et al. [4] proposed a recurrent neural network for classifying network traffic.
Although deep learning models can achieve high accuracy, their training and inference processes may require more computational resources than traditional machine-learning algorithms.
For small or resource-constrained environments, a lightweight model may therefore provide a practical alternative.
The approach presented in this paper focuses on reducing the number of input features while maintaining acceptable detection performance.
The proposed system consists of four main stages: traffic collection, feature extraction, model training, and intrusion classification.

Random Forest is an ensemble-learning algorithm that constructs multiple decision trees and combines their predictions.

For an input sample xx, the final prediction can be expressed as: y^=mode{h1(x),h2(x),...,hn(x)}\hat{y} = \operatorname{mode}\{h_1(x), h_2(x), ..., h_n(x)\} where hi(x)h_i(x) represents the prediction of the ii-th decision tree and nn is the total number of trees.
In this experiment, the Random Forest classifier is configured with 100 decision trees.
The maximum tree depth is limited to reduce unnecessary model complexity.
A small network intrusion dataset containing 10,000 network-flow records was used for evaluation.
The dataset contains two classes: normal traffic and malicious traffic.
The records were divided into training and testing sets using an 80:20 ratio.
Therefore, 8,000 records were used for training and 2,000 records were used for testing.
The model was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.

Accuracy is calculated as: Accuracy=TP+TNTP+TN+FP+FNAccuracy = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} where TPTP, TNTN, FPFP, and FNFN represent true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, respectively.
Table 1 presents the classification results obtained from the test dataset.
The results indicate that the proposed model can distinguish between normal and malicious traffic with an accuracy of 94.2%.
The precision and recall values are also relatively balanced, suggesting that the model does not strongly favor one type of classification error.
The computational cost of the model was also measured.
Training the classifier with 100 trees required approximately 2.8 seconds on a standard desktop computer, while classification of the testing set required less than one second.
The experiment demonstrates that a relatively small feature set can provide useful information for network intrusion detection.
This is particularly relevant for systems where computational resources are limited.
However, reducing the number of features may also remove information that is useful for detecting sophisticated attacks.
In addition, the dataset used in this experiment is relatively small and contains only two traffic classes.
Therefore, the reported results should not be interpreted as evidence that the proposed approach can detect all types of real-world attacks.
Future experiments should evaluate the approach using larger and more diverse datasets.
Additional features, such as TCP flags, inter-arrival time, and packet-size statistics, could also be investigated.
This paper presented a lightweight machine-learning approach for network intrusion detection.
The proposed system uses five network-flow features and a Random Forest classifier to distinguish normal traffic from malicious traffic.
Experimental results achieved an accuracy of 94.2%, with an F1-score of 93.3%.
These results suggest that a lightweight feature set can provide useful intrusion detection capability while keeping computational requirements relatively low.
Future work will focus on evaluating the approach with larger datasets, detecting multiple attack categories, and comparing Random Forest with other lightweight classification algorithms.
